Deliverable 05 · reflection

What the data supports—and what it cannot prove

The most useful insight was not a single “best” library. It was the mismatch between how differently students work and how unevenly space information is published.

The evidence supports

Comparison

  • Published features make some spaces visibly better fits for specific tasks.
  • Quiet, private areas and collaborative, technology-rich rooms form different clusters.
  • Accessibility, power, noise, and reservation metadata are not consistently listed across the sample.
  • Cabot and Lamont expand late-night options because official pages describe them as 24-hour libraries.
  • A standardized data template would make the existing directory more useful.

The evidence cannot prove

Outcomes

  • Which space students actually like most or rate most highly.
  • How crowded a room will be at a particular time.
  • Whether an unlisted amenity is absent.
  • Whether the sample represents every Harvard school or study environment.
  • Whether adding an amenity would cause better grades, wellbeing, or library use.

I would improve the project by pairing the official inventory with two privacy-preserving sources: periodic anonymous seat counts by broad time block and a short intercept survey asking students to rank space features. That would separate “what is published,” “what exists,” and “what students experience.” Until then, the dashboard should be read as a transparent decision aid and a metadata-quality audit—not as a definitive ranking.
